Because electric forces depend on distance, equal amounts of separated positive and negative charge need not produce cancelling forces on the nearby charge.
Link the relevant physical cause to the observation asked about. Naming a law alone does not explain why this particular result follows.

sup-068b880983a8ffee-w1:d.i.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

sup-068b880983a8ffee-w1:d.ii.hint: Try placing a positive test charge at a few points to check the proposed field direction.
notes: Electric field lines point from positive towards negative charges, and their tangent gives the local field direction. Closer lines represent a stronger field.
Magnetic field lines form continuous loops. Field lines do not cross, because the field has one direction at each point.

sup-1a1f11bfa06203b4-w1:c.ii.hint: Identify the geometry producing the field before choosing its formula or hand rule.
notes: For a long straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr); for a long ideal solenoid, B = μ₀nI. Here n is turns per unit length.
Use a right-hand grip rule with conventional current. Add fields as vectors, including cancellation between competing contributions.

sup-1a1f11bfa06203b4-w1:d.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).
A magnetic field alone does no work: the force is perpendicular to velocity. Reverse the force direction for a negative charge.

sup-1a1f11bfa06203b4-w1:e.hint: Find the angle between the conventional current and the magnetic field.
notes: A straight current-carrying segment experiences F = BIL sin θ. Use the length actually within the field.
Use the current direction for the force hand rule. The magnetic force is perpendicular to both current and field; a segment parallel to the field has no magnetic force.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w1:b.ii.hint: Keep the proton count, neutron count and total nucleon count separate.
notes: Isotopes share proton number Z but differ in neutron number. Stability depends on the neutron-to-proton balance and competition between nuclear attraction and proton repulsion.
Nuclear radius scales approximately as A^(1/3), giving roughly constant nuclear density. Outer electrons control chemical behaviour; the nucleus controls radioactive properties.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w1:d.i.hint: Distinguish a prediction for one nucleus from a statistical prediction for a large collection.
notes: Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random: the decay time of one nucleus cannot be predicted, but a large sample follows a statistical decay law.
Alpha, beta and gamma radiation differ in charge, ionization and penetration. Relate the stated observation to the physical property being tested, rather than treating all radiation as identical.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w1:d.ii.hint: Keep a separate account of nucleon number and electric charge on both sides of the decay.
notes: In alpha decay A decreases by 4 and Z by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton; in beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, with the appropriate emitted leptons.
Gamma emission changes nuclear energy without changing A or Z. Beta decay shares energy with a neutrino or antineutrino, giving a continuous beta spectrum.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w1:e.hint: Compare the total mass or binding energy of the initial particles with that of the final particles.
notes: Energy released is (mass_initial − mass_final)c². Equivalently, it is the increase in total binding energy, not simply the difference in binding energy per nucleon.
When given binding energy per nucleon, multiply by the nucleon number first. Keep atomic and nuclear masses consistent so electron masses cancel correctly.
